Kinship Systems. The culturally determined frameworks through which societies organize relationships between family members and define rights, obligations, and social identity through descent, marriage, and affinity. They are foundational to understanding how societies structure themselves and transmit property, status, and belonging.

Every society has a kinship system, though they vary dramatically in who counts as a relative, what obligations kinship entails, and how inheritance and property flow through families. Types of descent vary across societies. Some trace kinship through patrilineal descent along the father's line, others through matrilineal descent along the mother's line, and still others through bilateral or cognatic descent recognizing both parents. Exogamy, marriage outside one's group, and endogamy, marriage within one's group, are marriage rules embedded in kinship systems that regulate who can marry whom.

A. R. Radcliffe-Brown revolutionized kinship studies by analyzing kinship systems as functional structures that organized labor, inheritance, and alliance across generations. He showed kinship was not just genealogy but social roles. Claude Lévi-Strauss demonstrated that kinship systems embody deep structural patterns. Marriage rules and descent groups are not arbitrary but follow underlying logic, such as elementary structures of kinship. He found universal patterns beneath surface variation. Terminology variations distinguish different societies. Some languages distinguish paternal and maternal uncles with separate words while others group them. These terminological differences map onto descent rules and inheritance patterns.

Modern kinship anthropology examines how kinship systems adapt to migration, colonization, legal systems, and LGBTQ-plus relationships, showing kinship as dynamic and contextual. Fictive kinship through adoption and chosen families expands beyond blood and marriage. Cross-cultural study reveals that no society treats all relatives identically. Every society allocates duties, privileges, and status differentially based on relation type, distance, and gender. A. R. Radcliffe-Brown pioneered structural-functional analysis of kinship systems and revolutionized the field. Claude Lévi-Strauss identified deep structural patterns in kinship and marriage exchange, showing kinship systems as ordered systems. Family structure is the household and family arrangements within which kinship relations are lived and expressed. Marriage rules govern who marries whom, encoded in kinship systems and enforcing group alliance and exchange. Descent groups such as lineages, clans, and other groups formed through traced descent are basic units within kinship systems. Structural anthropology, the theoretical approach pioneered by Lévi-Strauss, sees kinship as structured exchange and alliance. Ritual marks kinship transitions through birth, marriage, and death, reinforcing kinship meanings and solidarity.
